# Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos: An Optimized Four-Component Research Agenda

The project should be organized as one linked, leakage-controlled sequence: two-player perception and tracking, player-associated technical-action recognition, context-conditioned tactical-intent recognition, and past-only prediction of the next hitter’s action. The strongest immediate contribution is therefore not an unsupported claim of a complete end-to-end system, but a reproducible singles-video benchmark and evaluation protocol that makes each handoff auditable.

The evidence supports the feasibility of individual links. Existing work demonstrates player localization, court-coordinate mapping, stroke recognition, tactical sequence analysis, and next-stroke forecasting. However, the supplied literature does not establish a single validated system that simultaneously maintains two player identities through broadcast occlusions, recognizes a harmonized technical taxonomy, infers calibrated tactical intent, and predicts subsequent actions without future-information leakage. The agenda below makes those missing interfaces explicit.

## Roadmap

The first section fixes the project scope and the distinction between observable events and inferred decisions. The four numbered sections then specify, for each component, its objective, inputs, outputs, labels, temporal unit, model alternatives, evaluation, and limitations. The integration section defines the shared data schema, source selection, annotation protocol, split design, licensing, reproducibility, and leakage controls. The final section prioritizes feasible contributions and sets staged validation gates.

## Project framing, scope, and optimization criteria

### Operational scope

The project title is **“Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos.”** Its population is singles badminton match and rally video: one player on each side of the court. The project itself does not restrict tournament, country, sex, age, competition level, historical period, viewpoint, camera type, or frame rate. Those variables should therefore be recorded as metadata and used for generalization analysis rather than silently excluded.

The [Badminton World Federation Laws of Badminton](https://extranet.bwf.sport/docs/document-system/81/1466/1470/Section%204.1%20-%20Laws%20of%20Badminton%20-%2029%20May%202023%20V2.1.pdf) provide useful operational units:

- a singles match has one player on each opposing side;
- a rally starts with service and ends when the shuttle ceases to be in play;
- a stroke is a racket movement intended to hit the shuttle.

The BWF laws also establish that the server and receiver hit alternately during a rally. Score state is therefore a legitimate contextual variable, provided that the score available before the current action is used and the future rally outcome is not accidentally included. A normal match is best of three games, and a game is normally won at 21 points, subject to the deuce rules. These definitions make the rally, stroke, acting player, preceding sequence, and pre-rally score natural annotation units.

The four components should be treated as distinct scientific questions:

| Component | Central question | Primary unit and output | Main validity requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos | Where are the two players, and which detection belongs to which player over time? | Frame-level boxes, persistent anonymous IDs, visibility, court coordinates, trajectories | Identity continuity must survive occlusion, camera motion, and court-end changes |
| 2. Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players | What observable technical action did which player perform, and when? | Player-linked hit event, action label, onset/offset interval, and attributes | The label must distinguish technique from placement, trajectory, and intent |
| 3. Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players’ Actions | What tactical function is most plausibly associated with the action given the available context? | Shot- or rally-level intent distribution, confidence, evidence cues, and optional rationale | Intent must be explicitly inferred, uncertain, and separated from outcome |
| 4. Prediction of Singles Players’ Subsequent Actions | What will the next hitter do, given only information available before that action? | Next-player identity, next technical action, probability distribution, and top-k alternatives | The cutoff, actor, horizon, and candidate action space must be causal and explicit |

### Research objectives

The optimized project should pursue five objectives.

First, it should create a player-centered representation. The player is the organizing entity for all later analysis; “top” and “bottom” are only temporary image positions. A player can change court ends, and a broadcast can pan, zoom, or cut.

Second, it should use a documented technical ontology rather than treating every dataset’s label vocabulary as interchangeable. Existing resources report six, ten, twelve, eighteen, twenty-nine, or thirty-five classes, but these counts encode different distinctions. A crosswalk and a preserved raw-label layer are essential.

Third, it should define tactical intent as an expert-annotated interpretation of observable evidence. A model must not be described as reading a player’s private mental state. It estimates a tactical function such as defending, transitioning, creating pressure, attacking, or disguising an action.

Fourth, it should make prediction genuinely prospective. A model that sees the opponent’s next stroke, a symmetric window around the target event, or the final rally outcome is performing offline recognition or outcome-conditioned analysis, not causal next-action prediction.

Fifth, it should evaluate robustness and practical cost together. Accuracy alone is insufficient when a model fails under near-net overlap, changes of viewpoint, rare actions, or a modest shift from elite broadcasts to practice footage. Latency, annotation effort, calibration, interpretability, and access constraints belong in the research design.

### Evidence status and limits

Several studies validate parts of this chain. Chu and Situmeang map player position to court coordinates, classify strokes, and then combine movement and stroke sequences for binary offensive/defensive strategy classification in singles video ([Chu and Situmeang](http://mmcv.csie.ncku.edu.tw/~wtchu/papers/2017ICMR-chu.pdf)). ShuttleNet uses rally progress and player information for future-stroke forecasting ([Wang et al., ShuttleNet](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/20341/20100)). FineBadminton connects structural parsing, technical actions, tactical semantics, and decision evaluation ([FineBadminton](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07554)). BadmintonVision combines detection, temporal recognition, trajectories, and descriptive Markov analysis, but explicitly characterizes its tactical findings as exploratory and correlational ([BadmintonVision](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s13102-026-02073-1_reference.pdf)).

Those results support the architecture of the agenda, not a claim that the complete four-component system has already been validated. In particular, the supplied evidence does not provide:

- a standardized badminton benchmark for persistent two-player identities under simultaneous occlusion and moving-camera broadcast motion;
- a project-specific, validated tactical-intent ontology;
- project-specific intent agreement and probability calibration;
- a causal validation showing that inferred intent is distinct from outcome-conditioned stroke transitions;
- one shared match-disjoint robustness and ablation protocol across all four components;
- end-to-end error propagation results from missed or switched tracks through action, intent, and prediction.

These are research targets, not missing reasons to omit the underlying analyses.

## 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos

### Research objective and scope boundary

The first component should be a player-centric perception task:

> Given a singles-video sequence, detect the two players, maintain two anonymous identities through every rally, estimate their positions in image and court coordinates, and expose visibility and uncertainty information for later action, intent, and prediction models.

The target identities should be anonymous within a match or rally, such as `P_A` and `P_B`. Named player identification is optional and should not be required for the core task. It introduces additional privacy, licensing, and generalization issues and is unnecessary for assigning a stroke to the correct side.

The tracker should not permanently define identities as `top` and `bottom`. Those labels are useful for a fixed-camera baseline, but they fail when players change ends or the camera changes. The system should maintain `P_A` and `P_B` through court-end changes, while also recording temporary screen position such as near-side or far-side.

The component should cover rally frames and the transitions immediately surrounding them. Full-match segmentation—rally, replay, challenge, interval, and advertisement—is useful, but it should be treated as a separate scene-status label rather than conflated with player tracking.

### Required inputs and outputs

The minimum input is RGB video plus frame timestamps and video metadata. The recommended output contract is:

| Output field | Required definition | Downstream use |
|---|---|---|
| Player box | Bounding box for each visible singles player in every evaluable frame | Detection, pose extraction, actor cropping |
| Persistent ID | Anonymous `P_A` or `P_B`, with tracklet and scene identifiers | Stroke association and sequence history |
| Visibility state | Fully visible, partially visible, heavily occluded, truncated, temporarily absent, or uncertain | Occlusion analysis and confidence-aware modeling |
| Court position | Feet or lower-body contact point mapped to court coordinates when homography is valid | Movement, opponent context, tactical features |
| Confidence and provenance | Detector confidence, association confidence, interpolation flag, and human-correction flag | Error propagation and auditability |

The tracker may additionally output pose keypoints and a shuttlecock trajectory, but these should remain separate streams. A shuttlecock detector is not a substitute for player tracking. One monocular shot-extraction study explicitly states that it does not track moving players across frames; it uses DensePose, perspective transformation, TrackNet, and swing detection to identify hit moments instead ([shot-extraction study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11244353/)). Shuttlecock tracking is justified here because it helps identify contact timing and flight context, not because it solves player identity.

Court lines and corners are also supporting entities. Their role is to estimate the homography and reject spectators or officials whose feet lie outside the playing area. They need not become persistent objects in the main player identity task.

### Annotation design

Each annotated frame should contain:

1. the box and anonymous identity of each player;
2. a visibility and truncation flag;
3. the visible fraction or occlusion category;
4. the lower-body point used for court mapping;
5. a camera-state label such as static, pan, tilt, zoom, replay, or cut;
6. an `ignore` region for spectators, referees, graphics, and other people likely to produce false detections.

Track recovery should be explicitly annotated. If a player disappears behind the opponent near the net, the data should record the last visible frame, the first reliable reappearance, whether the identity was recoverable, and whether an interpolated location is supplied. A tracker should not receive credit for a visually plausible interpolation if the identity was actually switched.

The project-specific standardized visibility thresholds are unavailable in the supplied evidence. They should therefore be fixed before evaluation, with examples for each category. The same thresholds must be used across all models.

### What existing studies establish

The literature illustrates both feasibility and the limits of current evidence.

The Badminton Olympic dataset manually annotated player boxes in selected frames, point segments, and 15,327 stroke annotations from ten 2012 Olympic matches involving twenty players. Its seven-training/three-test match split had no player overlap and is a useful precedent for generalization ([Ghosh, Singh, and Jawahar](https://cdn.iiit.ac.in/cdn/cvit.iiit.ac.in/images/ConferencePapers/2018/badminton_analytics.pdf)). However, the videos were restricted to behind-the-baseline views with minimal camera movement. Player identity was estimated by clustering foreground color histograms into two match-level groups, yielding 97.98% correspondence accuracy, but the authors caution that the method is not extensible when both players wear similar tournament clothing.

Chu and Situmeang used a fixed top/down arrangement, detected the largest connected component in the upper and lower halves, and mapped the bottom-border midpoint of each box to a court model. They report 85.45% player-detection accuracy and note that player shadows could be absorbed into the component, disturbing court position estimates. This is a useful low-complexity baseline, but it presupposes a stable camera and screen ordering ([Chu and Situmeang](http://mmcv.csie.ncku.edu.tw/~wtchu/papers/2017ICMR-chu.pdf)).

Nilesh et al. used `PlayerTop` and `PlayerBottom` classes in broadcast video. Their YOLOv3 detector reported mAP@0.5 of 98.07 for the top player and 98.13 for the bottom player, with a reported rally-processing latency of 0.14 seconds, compared with 96.90 and 97.85 for Faster R-CNN at 76.63 seconds ([Nilesh et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.12199v1)). These are useful detection and speed figures, but they do not establish persistent identity quality under occlusion. Their data also included doubles, where occlusion and blur were more frequent, so the reported numbers should not be treated as a singles MOT benchmark.

A six-video singles location-tracking study evaluated 334,654 frames and reported 321,235 recognized frames, or 95.86% frame-level recognition accuracy. Its failures concentrated at rally endings and when players overlapped near the net ([singles location-tracking study](https://doi.org/10.46669/kss.2022.20.1.075)). This result supports near-net overlap as a required test stratum, but frame recognition accuracy is not equivalent to HOTA, IDF1, or identity-switch rate.

A two-camera system assigns a top-view camera to trajectory tracking and a side-view camera to appearance features. It uses a 90-degree top view, CSRT tracking, appearance-based ReID, and perspective transformation to reconnect interrupted tracks ([two-camera badminton tracking](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.04872)). It demonstrates why a second view can help, but a two-camera setup should be an optional upper-bound condition, not a hidden requirement for the primary single-broadcast task.

### Model comparison

The comparison should separate detection, association, geometry, and deployment assumptions.

| Model family | Association mechanism | Appropriate baseline or extension | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed-view connected components or color clustering | Spatial ordering or appearance color | Reproduce the Ghosh and Chu style of low-cost fixed-camera analysis | Breaks under shadows, similar clothing, camera motion, and court-end changes |
| One-stage detector plus motion tracker | IoU, Kalman prediction, SORT, ByteTrack, or OC-SORT | Practical real-time baseline; compare YOLO-family detectors | Motion alone can switch identities during overlap |
| Detector plus appearance/ReID tracker | IoU and learned crop embeddings, such as BoT-SORT or DeepSORT-style association | Primary single-camera identity baseline | ReID can fail when players wear similar clothing or are blurred |
| Detector plus court registration and ground-plane motion | Homography, court landmarks, velocity prediction, camera-motion compensation | Robustness experiment for pans, zooms, and jitter | Requires reliable court geometry and a sufficiently planar playing surface |
| Multi-camera or end-to-end transformer tracker | Cross-view appearance, track queries, or long-term memory | Optional upper-bound and future extension | More equipment, annotation, computation, and licensing burden |

The 2025 singles-to-doubles transfer study provides a useful recovery mechanism: YOLOv11x and BoT-SORT use velocity extrapolation during missing detections, then restore an old ID when a reappearing detection lies within a 200-pixel radius of the predicted position. Missing periods were typically under ten frames in that study ([singles-to-doubles transfer study](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.13507v1)). The 200-pixel radius is source- and resolution-specific; it should not be transplanted as a universal badminton threshold. Its value is methodological: prediction, court ROI, and appearance should be evaluated as separate contributions.

Camera motion deserves its own ablation. General MOT work shows that ground-plane compensation and domain-adaptive appearance features can improve HOTA and IDF1 on moving-camera or difficult sports-like scenes, but those results are not badminton evidence. DCTrack reports HOTA 67.3% and IDF1 65.8% on DanceTrack, with combined domain adaptation and ground-plane compensation gains of 7.1 HOTA points on DanceTrack, 5.6 on MOT20, and 4.7 on MOT17 ([DCTrack](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics14112238)). FieldMOT similarly argues that field registration can remain robust to camera-motion noise, while noting that its homography assumes a flat field ([FieldMOT](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025W/CVSPORTS/papers/Chen_FieldMOT_A_Field-Registered_Multi-Object_Tracking_for_Sports_Videos_CVPRW_2025_paper.pdf)). These studies justify testing geometry and camera compensation, not claiming that their scores transfer to badminton.

### Evaluation

Detection should report AP or mAP at several IoU thresholds, preferably including 0.5 and a stricter threshold, together with precision, recall, and small-box performance. Detection alone should not be the primary component-1 result because a detector can produce accurate boxes while repeatedly assigning the wrong player identity.

The primary tracking metric should be HOTA, accompanied by:

- DetA for detection quality;
- AssA for association quality;
- LocA for localization quality;
- MOTA and MOTP for continuity with older literature;
- IDF1, ID precision, and ID recall;
- identity-switch count and track fragmentation;
- mostly-tracked and mostly-lost track rates;
- recovery time after occlusion;
- actor-assignment accuracy at annotated hit frames.

HOTA is appropriate because it balances detection, association, and localization rather than reducing the task to false detections and identity switches. The [TrackEval implementation](https://github.com/JonathonLuiten/TrackEval) supports HOTA, DetA, AssA, LocA, MOTA, MOTP, and IDF1, but a new badminton corpus requires format conversion or custom evaluator code.

Evaluation should be stratified by:

- full visibility versus partial or heavy occlusion;
- near-net overlap;
- shadows and similar clothing;
- static versus panning or zooming camera;
- overhead, rear-court, side-angle, and oblique views;
- native frame rate and resampled frame rate;
- broadcast graphics, replay, and court-adjacent spectators;
- player changes of court end.

The evaluation must report latency on named hardware. A model that produces strong offline tracks with a full-video smoother is not equivalent to an online tracker. Report detector time, association time, court-registration time, and total frames per second separately.

### Resulting judgment and limitation

The recommended component-1 contribution is a two-player, anonymous, match-disjoint tracking benchmark with visibility, court-coordinate, and hit-actor annotations. A YOLO-plus-OC-SORT or BoT-SORT baseline with court registration is a feasible starting point; ReID, camera compensation, and longer-term track recovery should be ablations rather than assumed necessities.

The evidence does not currently support a badminton-specific claim about persistent identities under simultaneous occlusion and moving-camera broadcast motion. That remains an explicit empirical question. A component-1 result should therefore report exactly where identity continuity fails instead of summarizing the system with one frame-level accuracy number.

## 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players

### Research objective

The second component should answer:

> Given the track of a player and the surrounding video, which observable technical action did that player perform, at what time, and with which optional execution and placement attributes?

Technical action is not tactical intent. A smash, clear, drop, or lift describes what the player did and, in some taxonomies, how the shuttle travelled. Whether the action was intended to attack, recover, deceive, or create pressure belongs to component 3.

The model should recognize a player-linked event even when both players appear in the same frame. A prediction without a reliable hitter identity is incomplete for singles analysis.

### A literature-grounded taxonomy catalogue

The existing resources should be treated as related but non-equivalent label systems.

#### Coarse and stroke-event taxonomies

| Source | Named action entries | Actor and granularity | Temporal treatment | Research value and limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Badminton Olympic | Serve, forehand, backhand, lob, smash for both top and bottom players, plus react and none | Player-position-specific; 12 classes | Stroke intervals and response segments | Provides player-linked labels and a match/player-disjoint split, but merges many techniques |
| Chu and Situmeang | Clear, drive, drop, lob, smash, others | Primarily bottom player; six classes | Framewise observations and play sequences | Useful coarse baseline; `others` merges remaining strokes and non-hitting frames |
| Wang et al., ShuttleNet | Net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, short service, long service | Ten domain-expert stroke types, with hitter identity | Stroke-level sequence records | Well suited to forecasting; source-specific and without a footwork label |
| ShuttleSet | Net shot, return net, smash, wrist smash, lob, defensive return lob, clear, drive, driven flight, back-court drive, drop, passive drop, push, rush, defensive return drive, cross-court net shot, short service, long service | One hitting-time/frame anchor, both player locations | Point event rather than true interval | Rich spatial and stroke history; its 18 labels are not interchangeable with other 18-class datasets |
| BFMD | Serve, long serve, smash, clear, drop, push, net shot, net kill, lift, drive, block, press | Shot-level, usually with broadcast-order player fields | Frame-precise hit events | Strong full-match and multimodal context; caption experiments use ground-truth events and do not evaluate upstream tracking |

The [ShuttleSet annotation schema](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.04948) stores the hitting frame, hitter, both players’ court locations, shuttle location and height, service or return status, forehand and around-the-head flags, and shot type. Its 18-class system is particularly valuable for a structured event representation.

BFMD’s [12-class taxonomy](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/CVsports/papers/Ding_BFMD_A_Full-Match_Badminton_Dense_Dataset_for_Dense_Shot_Captioning_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf) adds four trajectory or intensity attributes, three court regions, and three tactical-intent groups. The shot class is trained as a multi-label semantic description in its captioning task, which is useful evidence that a technical event and its attributes should not always be forced into one mutually exclusive label.

#### Fine-grained and auxiliary taxonomies

| Source | Named entries or hierarchy | Temporal and actor fields | Annotation strength | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VideoBadminton | Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, Short Flat Shot | Clip-level action labels with player location and shuttle trajectory | 18 fine-grained classes, 60 fps controlled capture, coach review | Practice footage, controlled ball feeding for rare actions, and access/licensing details not fully stated |
| FineBadminton | 11 primary hit types and 20 subtypes; examples include jump smash and slice smash; one stroke may have multiple subcategories | Hit-centered structured records and rally clips | Expert-informed hierarchical technical and tactical fields | The supplied evidence does not provide the complete list of all 11 primary labels |
| Fine-Badminton temporal benchmark | 29 categories; examples include Lift, High Clear, Drop Shot, Short Smash, Defensive Lift, Smash Return of Serve, and Flat Serve | Explicit onset and offset intervals | 31 professional singles matches, 25 fps, frame-level boundaries | A public Zenodo release contains only ten matches and 9,817 annotations |
| TactiPlay | Clear, smash, drop, drive, rush, push, lob, net shot, cross-court net shot, plus two serve types | 11-frame windows centered on a hit, with hitter and handside | Expert-derived nine-type shot taxonomy and event table | Shot classification required manual correction; evidence comes from seven amateur videos and a fixed rear-court view |
| Footwork auxiliary stream | Chasse-step, shuffle, split-step, half-lunge, forward-lunge, scissors kick | Player trajectory or pose sequence, not a stroke event | Observational singles research reports frequencies and stroke associations | Footwork labels should not be collapsed into the technical stroke class |

VideoBadminton reports 7,822 clips, 18 classes, 145 minutes of self-recorded practice footage, and 19 school-team players. It used five student labelers and review by a university head coach; the capture camera recorded 1280×960 at 60 fps from approximately two metres behind the baseline and 4.5 metres high ([VideoBadminton](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12385v1)). Its controlled ball-feeding augmentation is useful for rare-class coverage but should be marked because it changes the natural distribution of rallies.

The 2026 Fine-Badminton temporal-localization study is a different resource from the 2025 FineBadminton semantic dataset. It contains 31 professional singles matches, approximately 32.76 hours at 25 fps, 2,104 rallies, and 27,597 action intervals across 29 classes. The public [Zenodo subset](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20292976) contains ten matches, 980,703 frames, 9,817 annotations, and 29 categories. Its original videos remain subject to the rights of their owners and are distributed for non-commercial academic research.

### Recommended canonical ontology

The project should preserve every source label in its original form, but expose a common hierarchical head for cross-source comparison.

#### Level 1: primary technical family

Use one primary family per hit:

1. **Serve**
2. **Clear**
3. **Drop**
4. **Smash**
5. **Drive or flat shot**
6. **Lift or lob**
7. **Net shot, net kill, or rush**
8. **Push or block**
9. **Other, no-hit, react, or uncertain**

This is a proposed harmonized family layer, not a claim that the BWF laws prescribe these machine-learning classes. It covers the repeated concepts in the domain-expert taxonomies while keeping source-specific labels available.

#### Level 2: technical subtype and attributes

Attach zero or more attributes:

- short serve or long serve;
- wrist, tap, jump, or slice smash;
- defensive or attacking variant;
- forehand, backhand, or around-the-head;
- cross-court, straight, body, or passing trajectory;
- front-court, mid-court, or rear-court origin and target;
- high, downward, flat, soft, or steep trajectory;
- hit height relative to the net;
- return-of-serve or defensive-return status;
- handside and, where reliably visible, racket-side information.

A stroke can legitimately have multiple attributes. A slice smash, for example, should not be forced to choose between “smash” and “slice” when the first is the primary family and the second is an execution attribute. FineBadminton explicitly permits a stroke to belong to multiple subcategories.

#### Level 3: auxiliary movement

Footwork should be a separate output stream. It may include split step, chasse, shuffle, lunge, or recovery movement, but it should not be inserted as a competing stroke label. Abdullahi and Coetzee report per-match frequencies for chasse-step, shuffle, split-step, half-lunge, forward-lunge, and scissors kick and correlations between footwork and stroke use ([Abdullahi and Coetzee](https://doi.org/10.1080/24748668.2017.1303955)). Those correlations support a useful context stream, not a causal interpretation.

### Temporal boundaries and recognition granularity

The action representation should contain three separate temporal objects.

#### Contact event

The contact frame or contact time $`t_i`$ is the frame at which the racket hits the shuttle. This is the primary anchor for player association, event recognition, and next-action sequencing. The [BST study](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.21085v2) defines a stroke around a one-to-one hit frame and uses variable clips bounded by nearby opponent hits.

#### Action interval

The interval $`[t_{start}, t_{end}]`$ covers the observable preparation, execution, and immediate follow-through. The project should define onset as the first frame showing movement attributable to the stroke and offset as the final frame before recovery or the next distinct action. Ambiguous onset or offset should receive a boundary-quality flag.

This interval is a labeling decision, not an objective physical fact. It should be independently annotated and adjudicated. A fixed symmetric window may be useful for compatibility, but it is not a measured action boundary. Fine-Badminton provides interval annotations and evaluates temporal localization over tIoU thresholds from 0.3 to 0.7. In contrast, ShuttleSet lacks explicit boundaries; a recent study converts a point at frame $`t`$ into the approximate interval $`[t-9,t+9]`$, or 19 frames, which should not be presented as observed onset and offset ([Fine-Badminton temporal-localization study](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.23355)).

#### Recognition context window

A hit-centered window may include frames before and after contact for offline recognition. The window must be labeled as offline if it contains any part of the opponent’s future response. BST explicitly includes the beginning of the opponent’s next stroke in some clips, which is legitimate for offline recognition but future information for online prediction. The same model should therefore be evaluated with:

- an offline symmetric window;
- a causal window ending at the prediction cutoff;
- a short hit-centered window;
- a longer rally-context window.

### Single-label, multilabel, and rare-action policy

The recommended policy is:

- one primary technical family per hit;
- multilabel subtype and execution attributes;
- an explicit `uncertain` or `not inferable` state;
- `none` or `react` only for continuous-stream segmentation, not as a way to hide unrecognized technical actions.

This separation prevents a taxonomy from becoming artificially precise. It also allows the model to predict that an event is a smash with high confidence but that its exact subtype is uncertain.

Class imbalance is a central design issue. ShuttleSet reports large differences between frequent and rare types: its table contains thousands of net shots but only 43 driven-flight examples, with none for women’s singles in that category. BST reports that driven flight had fewer than 50 instances and was merged into `none`; another ShuttleSet cleaning procedure merged push and lob, each with fewer than 50 instances, into `push lob`, and wrist smash into smash. These choices may be practical, but they change the task and must be declared before test evaluation.

Fine-Badminton gives a clearer long-tail example: Lift has 5,700 instances, or 20.65%, whereas Flat Serve has 58, or 0.21%, and Smash Return of Serve has 88, or 0.32%. Its DSTA model uses focal loss for hard and rare examples ([Fine-Badminton temporal-localization study](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.23355)).

The project should therefore report:

- macro-F1 and weighted-F1;
- balanced accuracy and mean class accuracy;
- per-class recall, especially for rare actions;
- minimum-class F1 or worst-quartile performance;
- top-1 and top-k accuracy;
- confusion among neighboring classes;
- performance before and after any pre-registered class merge.

A class should not be merged merely because the model performs poorly on it. First report the original class, its support, and its uncertainty. If a merge is necessary, report both the original-label result and the merged-label result.

### Model comparison

The component should compare model families on the same player-associated events and splits.

| Family | Input | Output | Strength | Main comparison question |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HOG/SVM or shallow CNN | Cropped player frames and short optical-flow features | Coarse stroke class | Transparent, inexpensive baseline; Chu used HOG and SVM | How much does temporal modeling add? |
| 3D CNN or two-pathway video model | RGB clip | Technical class | R(2+1)D, SlowFast, VideoMAE, and related models capture motion | Does RGB resolve rapid action differences? |
| Skeleton model | Player poses and bones | Technical class and actor | ST-GCN, PoseC3D, and TemPose reduce background dependence | How robust is pose to viewpoint and missing joints? |
| Multimodal temporal model | Pose, court position, shuttle trajectory, RGB | Technical class and attributes | BST and TemPose show gains from player and shuttle context | Which cue resolves which confusion? |
| Temporal action-localization model | Untrimmed video | Class plus onset/offset | ActionFormer/DSTA-style models address continuous rally localization | Can the system locate actions rather than classify pre-cut clips? |

VideoBadminton’s balanced-subset benchmark illustrates why the comparison should be data-specific. On its 50-sample-per-class subset, the reported Top-1/Top-5/mean-class accuracies were 82.80%/97.54%/73.80% for SlowFast, 81.99%/96.52%/69.93% for Swin, 80.76%/96.01%/67.18% for PoseC3D, 74.41%/93.76%/61.44% for ST-GCN, and 14.23%/62.23%/10.76% for MViT-V2 under that study’s particular configuration ([VideoBadminton benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12385v2)). These values are not universal rankings: they depend on the small practice corpus, sample selection, training settings, and label definition.

TemPose provides a more direct multimodal comparison. On the Badminton Olympics dataset, its temporal fusion version reached 90.7% top-1 accuracy with court position and shuttle position, compared with 85.6% for its skeleton-only version; on the confidential placement dataset, its interaction-fusion version reached 84.3% versus 83.9% for temporal fusion ([TemPose](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023W/CVSports/papers/Ibh_TemPose_A_New_Skeleton-Based_Transformer_Model_Designed_for_Fine-Grained_Motion_CVPRW_2023_paper.pdf)). The result supports ablations over player position and shuttle information, but the datasets and splits differ from a new project corpus.

BST’s ShuttleSet ablation similarly supports multimodal comparison. A fixed-width BST configuration using joint/bone pose, shuttlecock position, and player position reported accuracy 0.8254, Macro-F1 0.7983, minimum-class F1 0.5196, and top-2 accuracy 0.9503, compared with ST-GCN at 0.7758, 0.7352, 0.3726, and 0.9200. The proposed clipping strategy raised the BST values to 0.8322, 0.8097, 0.5762, and 0.9594 ([BST](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/CVsports/papers/Chang_BST_Badminton_Stroke-type_Transformer_for_Skeleton-based_Action_Recognition_in_Racket_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf)). These are stroke-recognition results, not tracking or next-action results.

### Evaluation and error analysis

Technical recognition should be evaluated at two levels.

At the event level, report top-1, top-k, macro-F1, per-class recall, balanced accuracy, calibration, and actor-association accuracy. At the interval level, report temporal mAP across tIoU thresholds, average boundary error, and missed, split, merged, and duplicate events.

Errors should be grouped by mechanism:

- forehand versus backhand when the racket is blurred;
- clear versus lift or lob when shuttle height is not visible;
- drop versus net shot when the contact frame is missed;
- drive versus flat shot or push;
- smash versus tap or jump smash;
- serve versus early preparation;
- technical class confusion caused by a wrong player ID;
- rare action failure caused by insufficient support;
- boundary error caused by fixed windows;
- action recognition that succeeds only because the opponent’s future response is visible.

The primary result should be the match- and player-disjoint test result. A model trained and tested on clips from the same match may exploit camera layout, clothing, player style, or near-duplicate frames. Within-match scores can be reported as a secondary diagnostic but should not be used as the principal generalization claim.

### Resulting judgment and limitation

The optimized technical-recognition task is hierarchical, actor-linked, and explicitly temporal. A practical first milestone is a canonical primary-family head plus source-specific subtype heads, trained on reliable contact events and evaluated both offline and causally. A 29-class end-to-end system may be a later extension; forcing all data into a single fine-grained vocabulary before identity and boundary quality are stable would increase annotation cost without necessarily improving scientific validity.

## 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players’ Actions

### Observable technique versus inferred intent

Tactical intent is not directly visible in the same way as a bounding box or contact frame. It is an interpretation of why an action is tactically useful in its situation. The project should define intent as:

> An expert judgment about the tactical function of an observable action, conditional on player position, opponent position, score state, preceding actions, shuttle trajectory, and rally phase.

This definition avoids claiming that a model has recovered a player’s private mental state. It also prevents the rally winner from being treated as proof that an earlier action was “intended” to win.

The distinction is important:

- **Technique:** what the player did;
- **Placement and trajectory:** where and how the shuttle travelled;
- **Tactical intent:** the inferred function of the action in context;
- **Outcome:** whether the rally was won, lost, or ended by a particular error.

The same technical action can have different tactical functions. A clear can be defensive recovery, neutral reset, or deliberate pressure through depth. A drop can be an attack, a transition, a disguise, or an emergency response.

### Existing intent and strategy vocabularies

The literature offers useful ingredients but not a common ontology.

| Source | Named intent or strategy entries | Unit and context | Evidence contribution | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chu and Situmeang | Offensive or defensive | Framewise stroke type plus bottom-player court region; two HMMs | Provides a direct sequence model and likelihood-based classification | Binary labels omit deception, transition, pressure, score, and uncertainty |
| BFMD | Attack/aggressive/finish; defensive/recover/reset; pressure/disrupt | Shot-level multimodal description; multi-label semantic attributes | Explicitly separates technical shot, trajectory, court region, and intent groups | Caption-oriented experiments use ground-truth events and do not validate end-to-end intent recognition |
| FineBadminton | Deception, defensive play, passive/transitional shot, plus nine strategic classifications and shot characteristics | Stroke and rally hierarchy with position and outcome fields | Richest supplied semantic structure for intent-like annotation | The paper characterizes intent as subjective and does not establish project-specific agreement or calibration |
| TactiPlay | Technical Execution; Positioning and Recovery; Tactical Choices | Stroke, three-stroke chunk, prefix, terminal, and rally units | Expert commentary traces how the preceding two shots influenced the current action | Seven amateur videos, fixed rear-court view, and no reported intent-specific agreement |
| BadmintonVision | Outcome-associated transition signatures such as forehand-to-jump-smash and backhand-to-backhand | Rally-level Markov matrices separated by scoring and conceding | Demonstrates descriptive sequence analysis and explicit caution about correlation | It is not a validated intent ontology and uses only five object/action classes |
| Liu et al. and Shishido and Nishijima | Tactical combinations based on technique, start/target placement, opponent position, and movement | Nine-cell court grid, stroke sequences, split-step and placement context | Provides measurable spatial and movement context | These studies do not directly label calibrated latent intent |

Chu and Situmeang quantize the bottom half of the court into nine regions and feed stroke type plus region into two offensive/defensive HMMs. Automatically extracted features achieved 70% average strategy accuracy, while manually corrected features achieved 83.33% in their five-fold evaluation ([Chu and Situmeang](http://mmcv.csie.ncku.edu.tw/~wtchu/papers/2017ICMR-chu.pdf)). The gap is important: tactical classification inherits upstream tracking and stroke errors.

FineBadminton’s [Tactical Semantics](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07554) includes straight-line and cross-court trajectory, passing, body and overhead shots, out-of-bounds and net outcomes, deception, defensive play, and passive or transitional shot descriptions. Its hierarchy is highly useful for annotation design, but the supplied evidence does not establish that its nine strategic classifications form a validated, mutually exclusive intent ontology.

BFMD defines three broad intent groups—attack, defense, and pressure—and trains semantic attributes with multi-label binary cross-entropy. This is a useful model for overlapping labels, because a shot can pressure an opponent while also preparing an attack ([BFMD](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/CVsports/papers/Ding_BFMD_A_Full-Match_Badminton_Dense_Dataset_for_Dense_Shot_Captioning_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf)).

TactiPlay’s expert process is particularly relevant to temporal granularity. Three national-level players with more than ten years of competitive and coaching experience annotated seven approximately eight-minute amateur videos and produced 304 issues. The analysis considers the preceding two shots, one- or two-stroke opening prefixes, three-stroke tactical chunks, and terminal units consisting of the final three strokes or fewer ([TactiPlay](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.27125)). These units should be adapted for the project, while recognizing that the source’s narrow population and fixed viewpoint limit generalization.

### Recommended provisional intent ontology

The project should publish a provisional ontology before annotation, rather than selecting intent labels after model inspection.

#### Primary tactical function

Use a multi-label strategic-function layer:

- **Defensive/recover/reset:** regain time, height, or court balance under pressure;
- **Neutral/build/transition:** maintain the rally or move from defense toward attack;
- **Pressure/disrupt:** constrain the opponent, alter rhythm, target the body, or force a difficult movement;
- **Attack/finish:** exploit an opportunity to end the rally or produce a weak return;
- **Deception/disguise:** conceal or disguise direction, pace, or stroke intention;
- **Uncertain/not inferable:** insufficient evidence or disagreement too large for a reliable label.

The first four labels describe tactical function; deception is an orthogonal execution-purpose tag and should be allowed to co-occur with attack, pressure, or transition. `Uncertain` is not a failure label. It records that the video and context do not support a defensible inference.

#### Tactical-purpose attributes

Where annotation quality permits, add multi-label tags:

- move the opponent to a target region;
- exploit an open or weakly covered area;
- target the body or racket side;
- change pace or trajectory;
- force a lift or high return;
- protect recovery position;
- maintain central court control;
- create an opportunity for the next stroke.

These are proposed operational labels informed by the spatial evidence in Liu et al., Shishido and Nishijima, and the expert structures in FineBadminton and TactiPlay. They are not established facts about player psychology.

### Shot-level and rally-level units

Intent should be annotated at more than one temporal scale.

#### Shot-level intent

For each hit $`i`$, record:

- the observable technical label;
- start and target court zones;
- hitter and opponent positions;
- preceding action history;
- pre-rally score and game phase;
- shuttle height or trajectory when reliable;
- one or more tactical-function labels;
- confidence and a short evidence rationale.

The label should be based on the context available up to the hit for the prospective version. A separate retrospective version may use the complete rally, but it must be marked as hindsight annotation.

#### Short-sequence intent

Use the preceding two strokes as one context condition, following TactiPlay, and use three-stroke chunks to capture action-response-outcome patterns. These units are useful for recognizing a transition such as defend–lift–attack without claiming that every three-stroke segment is a complete tactic.

#### Rally-level intent

For a rally, summarize opening, middle, and terminal phases. The terminal unit can contain the last three strokes or fewer when the rally ends earlier. Outcome may be included in a retrospective rally summary, but outcome must not be fed to a prospective model that is meant to recognize intent before the rally ends.

### Context features

The minimum context feature groups should be evaluated separately:

1. **Technical:** current and preceding shot family, subtype, handside, and hit height.
2. **Spatial:** hitter position, opponent position, start zone, target or landing zone, and court-region transitions.
3. **Opponent:** opponent recovery position, distance to likely contact point, movement direction, and whether the opponent is near the baseline, net, or side boundary.
4. **Shuttle:** two-dimensional trajectory, height, speed proxy, and landing location when confidence is adequate.
5. **Score and game:** pre-rally score, game point phase, server/receiver status, and game number.
6. **Rally history:** preceding two or three strokes, rally length, and phase.
7. **Player style:** optional identity or style embedding, evaluated separately on seen and unseen players.

Score is context, not proof of intent. Player identity or style can improve prediction but can also conceal a failure to generalize. Every experiment should state whether player identity is available.

### Annotation protocol and uncertainty

The annotation interface should separate evidence from inference. For each shot, the annotator should first enter observable fields and only then select intent labels. The interface should display:

- current and preceding strokes;
- both player trajectories;
- opponent and hitter positions;
- score before the rally;
- shuttle trajectory or landing area, with missing-data indicators;
- a short temporal window around the hit;
- the annotator’s confidence;
- an optional rationale tied to visible evidence.

At least two independent annotators should label every intent sample. A senior badminton annotator should adjudicate disagreements, and a third expert should review a stratified sample of difficult, rare, and ambiguous cases. The protocol should include an explicit `not inferable` option so that annotators are not forced to agree on an interpretation.

The supplied evidence provides precedents but not a project result. FineBadminton uses two independent annotators with senior review; BFMD has at least three reviewers with more than five years of badminton experience for captions; BadmintonVision reports Cohen’s kappa of 0.89 on 500 images for object/action labels; and a youth-championship study reports κ greater than 0.85 for all coded variables, although that paper contains an internal conflict in its match counts. None of these values is intent-specific for the proposed project.

Agreement should be reported separately from reliability. [Liao, Hunt, and Chen](https://doi.org/10.47102/annals-acadmedsg.v39n8p613) emphasize that raters can agree within an individual but be inconsistent across individuals. [McHugh](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3900052/) notes that percent agreement is interpretable but ignores chance agreement, while Cohen’s kappa accounts for chance under its assumptions.

The project should therefore report:

- percent agreement;
- Cohen’s or weighted kappa for categorical primary intent;
- Krippendorff’s alpha or multilabel agreement for overlapping tags;
- agreement by class and ambiguity stratum;
- annotator confidence distributions;
- the adjudication rate;
- the proportion labeled `uncertain`;
- the empirical expert-agreement ceiling.

The project-specific intent ontology, intent-specific inter-rater results, and calibrated uncertainty results are not available in the supplied evidence. They must be measured rather than inferred from general action-label agreement.

### Model alternatives

The comparison should proceed from interpretable sequence models to multimodal neural models.

A rule-based or structured baseline can classify defensive, neutral, pressure, or attack functions from action family, court position, target region, and opponent location. It establishes whether a complex model adds value over obvious spatial rules.

A binary HMM reproduces the Chu baseline. A multi-state HMM or conditional Markov model can represent transitions among defense, transition, pressure, and attack, while exposing state likelihoods and transition contributions.

Tree-based models such as logistic regression, random forest, or gradient boosting can test structured context and provide feature-importance baselines. Their explanations should be treated as associations, not causal effects.

A temporal LSTM or Transformer can model preceding strokes, trajectories, and positions. A graph or interaction Transformer can represent the hitter and opponent as two interacting actors. A multimodal model can fuse RGB, pose, court coordinates, shuttle trajectory, and score.

An MLLM or VLM may assist annotation or provide a comparison system for descriptive reasoning, but it should not be treated as validated intent ground truth. FineBadminton’s FBBench results show that even strong multimodal models find deep badminton reasoning difficult: the best reported multiple-choice score in the supplied table is 42.06% for a fine-tuned Qwen2.5VL-7B configuration, and the benchmark authors state that current MLLMs still face substantial challenges ([FineBadminton](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07554)).

### Evaluation and interpretability

Intent recognition requires more than accuracy.

For mutually exclusive primary intent, report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, and confusion matrices. For multilabel tactical-purpose tags, report micro- and macro-F1, label-wise average precision, Jaccard similarity, and subset accuracy with care about its strictness.

Because the output is uncertain, report:

- cross-entropy or negative log-likelihood;
- Brier score;
- expected calibration error;
- reliability diagrams;
- calibration by class and confidence stratum;
- selective risk when the model abstains;
- agreement between model rationales and expert evidence fields.

For interpretability, HMM likelihoods and transition contributions are directly inspectable. Tree models can provide feature importance and SHAP summaries, but these should be checked against controlled ablations. Attention maps can show which frames the model uses, but attention alone is not a causal explanation. The temporal-attention analysis in TemPose is best treated as a diagnostic that the model emphasizes action-relevant frames, not proof that a particular cue caused a tactical decision.

A critical validity test is to compare:

1. a model using only observable current action and position;
2. a model adding opponent position;
3. a model adding preceding actions;
4. a model adding score;
5. a model adding shuttle trajectory;
6. an outcome-conditioned retrospective model;
7. a prospective model with outcome hidden.

If the outcome-conditioned model performs much better but the prospective model does not, the correct conclusion is that the system recognizes outcome-associated patterns rather than validated intent.

### Resulting judgment and limitation

The tactical component should be framed as calibrated, context-conditioned intent recognition with an explicit abstention option. The strongest feasible contribution is a carefully annotated shot- and rally-level intent resource that distinguishes evidence from interpretation and reports uncertainty. The project should not claim causal intent or mental-state recognition unless a separate design can test those claims. The supplied literature supports candidate labels and context features, but not a finalized ontology or causal validity result.

## 4) Prediction of Singles Players’ Subsequent Actions

### Target definition

The fourth component should answer:

> After an observed stroke and before the next stroke occurs, what technical action will the next hitter perform?

The predicted actor is therefore the next hitter in the turn-based rally, not an unspecified player and not necessarily the player whose current stroke was just recognized. The BWF order-of-play rule makes the next actor identifiable from the rally sequence, subject to correct stroke-event and identity annotations.

The primary target should be the next technical action. Rally winner, point outcome, and final score should be separate tasks. A model that predicts whether a player wins the rally may be useful for tactical analysis, but it is not a next-action model.

### Recommended prediction contract

| Field | Recommended specification | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Predicted player | The player who will hit the next valid stroke, represented as `P_A` or `P_B` | Preserves actor identity and prevents match-level ambiguity |
| Primary horizon | One next stroke | Gives a clear causal target and avoids compounding uncertainty |
| Extended horizon | Next $`n`$ strokes, reported separately | Matches ShuttleNet and ShuttleSet22 but requires sequence-level evaluation |
| Information cutoff | Immediately after the last observed stroke for the primary task; optional fixed lead time before the target hit for anticipation | Prevents future-stroke and post-hit leakage |
| Candidate space | The canonical technical-action family, with optional subtype and target-zone heads | Keeps prediction aligned with component 2 |
| Output | Full probability distribution, top-1, and top-k candidates | Badminton decisions are inherently multimodal |
| Secondary output | Target court region or landing area | Separates action choice from destination prediction |
| Excluded target | Rally winner or point outcome | Outcome prediction is a distinct task |

The primary one-step task should use a causal cutoff immediately after the observed stroke. The model may see the completed observed stroke, the score before the rally, and all previous representations, but it must not see any frame, label, or feature from the target stroke or the opponent’s future response.

For action anticipation, define fixed lead-time conditions such as 100 ms, 200 ms, and 400 ms before the target contact, subject to the native frame rate and sufficient samples. These are proposed operating points, not reported findings. The evaluation must state whether the model is predicting at the observed-stroke cutoff or at a pre-contact anticipation cutoff.

A second extension can predict the next $`n`$ strokes. In that case, report one-step performance separately from free-running multi-step performance. Teacher forcing, in which the ground-truth previous action is supplied at each step, should not be confused with deployment-style forecasting from the model’s own previous predictions.

### Candidate action space

The forecast head should use the same canonical family layer as technical recognition:

- serve, with short/long subtype;
- clear;
- drop;
- smash;
- drive or flat shot;
- lift or lob;
- net shot, net kill, or rush;
- push or block;
- other or uncertain.

A finer head can predict the source-specific 10-, 18-, or 29-class vocabulary, but the mapping must be published. If destination is predicted, use a nine-cell court grid or continuous coordinates as a separate output. Liu et al. use a 3×3 court grid, and ShuttleNet and ShuttleSet22 provide shot-type and area-coordinate forecasting formulations.

A hierarchical output is preferable to an artificially precise flat classifier:

1. predict primary action family;
2. predict subtype when the family is sufficiently supported;
3. predict target region or continuous landing location;
4. return calibrated uncertainty and an abstention option.

### Evidence from subsequent-action and related prediction studies

ShuttleNet defines forecasting from observed strokes and their hitting players to future strokes, including shot types and area coordinates. Its location output uses a probabilistic formulation because returns can be uncertain and multimodal ([ShuttleNet](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/20341/20100)). The reported 75-match corpus contains 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, and 43,191 strokes, with the first 80% of each match’s rallies used for training and the remainder for testing with five-fold cross-validation. This is a valuable forecasting precedent, but it is not a match- and player-disjoint generalization protocol.

ShuttleSet22 formulates the task with $`\tau=4`$ observed strokes and predicts the next $`n`$ strokes’ shot types and area coordinates. Teams generate six sequences per rally; the challenge evaluates shot type by cross-entropy and area coordinates by mean absolute error, selecting the sequence closest to ground truth ([ShuttleSet22](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15664v3)). The closest-sequence rule is useful for a stochastic challenge but can reward a lucky sample, so the proposed project should also report the full predictive distribution’s likelihood and calibration.

RallyTemPose uses a Transformer encoder-decoder with court position, skeleton pose, player embeddings, and turn-based actor/reactor context to predict the next stroke. It reports top-2 and top-3 accuracy because multiple strokes can be viable ([RallyTemPose](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024W/CVsports/papers/Ibh_A_Stroke_of_Genius_Predicting_the_Next_Move_in_Badminton_CVPRW_2024_paper.pdf)). Its paper describes 42 matches and 26 players, whereas the ShuttleSet release reports 44 matches and 27 players. These should be retained as distinct reported scopes rather than merged into one count.

TemPose-TF-ASF provides an important leakage-control design. Its two-stage contextual refinement uses preliminary predictions as estimated adjacent-stroke context instead of ground-truth future strokes. It reports 0.854 accuracy, 0.761 Macro-F1, and 0.945 top-2 accuracy on its ShuttleSet setting, compared with 0.835, 0.742, and 0.927 for TemPose-TF ([TemPose-TF-ASF](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.02558v3)). Its causal Transformer mask restricts each time step to the current and previous strokes. This is a useful design precedent, although the reported task is primarily stroke recognition with contextual refinement and should not automatically be described as an end-to-end raw-video forecast.

SPADE-LSTM offers a structured sequence baseline. It mines sequential patterns and feeds them to an LSTM using match–set–rally grouping to reduce information leakage. Its ten-class action-by-player task reports 88.68% accuracy and weighted F1 of 0.8851, with errors concentrated in tactically similar transitions and minority classes ([SPADE-LSTM](https://ijadis.org/index.php/ijadis/article/view/1510)). The result is not a raw-video result, but the split design and minority-class analysis are directly relevant.

### Comparison with outcome prediction

Several studies predict outcomes rather than the next action.

Yuan et al. use the number of strikes, scoring and losing location, techniques in the last three strokes, and serving location to predict scoring or losing situations. Their data were randomly split 90%/10%, and an RBF-kernel SVM reached 87.5% accuracy ([Yuan et al.](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0312801)). The study is useful for feature design and illustrates the distinction: its target is point outcome, not the next technical action.

BadmintonDB contains rally, stroke, and outcome annotations for nine matches between two top players and provides player-independent and player-dependent Naive Bayes outcome baselines ([BadmintonDB](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3552437.3555696)). ShuttleSet separates shot influence—predicting rally winner—from stroke forecasting and movement forecasting. Its ShuttleScorer reports AUC 0.8371, accuracy 0.7869, and Brier score 0.1574 on the shot-influence task, but those values cannot be compared with next-stroke accuracy ([ShuttleSet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.04948)).

The project should report these as neighboring outcome tasks, not substitute them for subsequent-action prediction.

### Model comparison

The minimum forecasting comparison should include:

1. **Majority and last-action baselines.** Predict the most frequent next action globally, by player, by current action, and by current action plus court zone.
2. **Empirical transition model.** Estimate $`P(a_{i+1}\mid a_i)`$ and progressively condition on player, position, opponent position, score, and rally phase.
3. **HMM or Markov model.** Provide interpretable state transitions and a probabilistic baseline.
4. **LSTM or GRU.** Establish a recurrent sequential baseline using the preceding stroke history.
5. **ShuttleNet-style model.** Separate rally-progress and player-style representations, then fuse them.
6. **RallyTemPose or causal multimodal Transformer.** Combine action history, poses, player positions, opponent context, and shuttle information with a causal mask.
7. **Raw-video model.** Use player tracks and video features directly, evaluated both with oracle event boundaries and predicted event boundaries.

The raw-video model should not be allowed to hide upstream errors. Report:

- oracle tracks and oracle technical labels;
- predicted tracks and oracle technical labels;
- oracle tracks and predicted technical labels;
- all predicted representations.

The difference between these conditions quantifies error propagation from components 1 and 2.

### Evaluation

For discrete next-action prediction, report:

- top-1 accuracy;
- top-3 and top-5 accuracy;
- macro-F1 and per-class recall;
- mean reciprocal rank;
- cross-entropy or negative log-likelihood;
- Brier score;
- expected calibration error and reliability diagrams;
- performance at each anticipation lead time;
- performance by player, action, court zone, rally phase, and score context.

Top-k output is not merely a convenience. Badminton players may have several viable responses, and a model can be useful if it identifies a small, well-calibrated set of plausible actions even when top-1 is wrong.

For location prediction, report area accuracy for a discrete grid and MAE for continuous coordinates. If a probabilistic coordinate model is used, report negative log-likelihood or coverage of prediction regions rather than only the closest sampled trajectory.

For sequence prediction, report one-step results first, then multi-step free-running results. The number of predicted steps must be fixed or explicitly conditioned on rally length. A model should not receive the actual remaining rally length unless that information would be available at deployment.

### Failure cases and limits

Forecasting will fail or become intrinsically uncertain when:

- the shuttle is out of view or lost during occlusion;
- the target player’s preparation is hidden by the opponent;
- the camera is distant, panning, or interrupted by a replay;
- several actions are physically plausible from the same state;
- rare action classes have little support;
- the player’s style changes with fatigue, score, opponent, or competition level;
- the input uses a switched identity or a future-smoothed trajectory;
- the target is defined at a finer granularity than the video can support.

Nokihara et al. show that adding player positions and poses improves shuttlecock trajectory prediction over shuttle-only input, but they also report failures when people occlude a distant camera or the shuttle leaves the field of view ([Nokihara et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2313-433X/9/5/99)). This supports player and pose ablations in component 4, but trajectory prediction is not the same as technical-action prediction.

### Resulting judgment and limitation

The primary contribution should be a one-step, next-hitter, past-only forecast with calibrated probabilities and a documented action vocabulary. Multi-step prediction, landing-area prediction, and rally-outcome prediction should be separate outputs. The strongest existing baselines operate on structured stroke histories rather than raw video, so the project can make a meaningful contribution by measuring the added value—and the error cost—of deriving those histories automatically from video.

## Cross-component architecture, data design, and validation

### Shared representation and handoffs

The four components should share a versioned event schema rather than passing opaque model embeddings.

| Representation | Produced by | Consumed by | Leakage control |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player track | Component 1 | Technical recognition, intent, prediction | Online identity may use only past frames; offline smoothing must be flagged |
| Technical event | Component 2 | Intent and next-action prediction | Contact and interval must be available only when their temporal definition permits |
| Tactical context | Components 1–3 | Intent and prediction | Score is pre-action; rally outcome is excluded from prospective inputs |
| Intent distribution | Component 3 | Optional forecast auxiliary head and analysis | Use only the intent estimate available at the cutoff, not a hindsight label |
| Forecast target | Component 4 | Evaluation only | The target action, future location, and future outcome never enter the input |

A useful canonical record contains:

- video, match, game, and rally identifiers;
- source URL or local asset identifier;
- frame index and timestamp;
- native and normalized frame rate;
- camera and viewpoint metadata;
- `P_A` and `P_B` boxes, visibility, confidence, and court position;
- optional pose keypoints and shuttle coordinates with confidence;
- hit frame, onset, offset, acting player, and technical labels;
- score before the rally and server/receiver status;
- intent labels, confidence, rationale, and annotator provenance;
- rally outcome, stored as a future field that is inaccessible to prospective models.

### Online and offline settings

The project should publish two explicit operating modes.

#### Offline analysis

Offline analysis can use the complete rally, bidirectional temporal encoders, track smoothing, and retrospective intent labels. It is appropriate for post-match coaching and descriptive statistics. Its results should not be presented as real-time anticipation.

#### Online or causal analysis

Online analysis processes frames in chronological order. It cannot use:

- the opponent’s future stroke;
- frames after the target action;
- a future-corrected identity assignment;
- the final rally outcome;
- an interval boundary determined after the action has ended;
- a target label used to build the input window.

The same model can be evaluated in both settings, but the settings must be reported separately. The BST clip design and the symmetric 19-frame conversion used for ShuttleSet temporal localization demonstrate why this distinction is necessary.

### Suitable data sources

No single existing resource satisfies all four components. A practical corpus strategy is to use one primary singles corpus with common annotations and treat other datasets as external tests or complementary sources.

| Resource | Coverage and annotations | View and frame information | Best use | Access and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Badminton Olympic | 10 matches, 20 players, boxes, point segments, 15,327 strokes, 12 coarse classes | Behind-baseline, minimal camera movement; frame rate not stated in supplied evidence | Player boxes, coarse action, player-disjoint baseline | Narrow viewpoint; identity method depends on appearance clusters |
| ShuttleSet | Reported release: 44 matches, 27 players, 3,685 rallies, 36,492 strokes; 18 shot types, both-player locations and shuttle fields | 1280×720, 30 fps; stadium-dependent camera variation | Technical history and forecasting | No predefined train/validation/test split; licensing and privacy protocol not stated |
| ShuttleSet22 | 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies, plus validation and test counts; $`\tau=4`$ forecasting formulation | Public competition video; frame rate not stated in supplied evidence | Next-action and location forecasting | Match- and player-disjoint status not stated; video license and reproducibility package unavailable in supplied evidence |
| FineBadminton, semantic release | 120 singles matches, 3,215 rally clips, 33,325 strokes; 11 primary types, 20 subtypes, tactical semantics and evaluation | 720p or higher, 25 fps; mainly overhead rear-court with some side-angle footage | Technical hierarchy, context, intent annotation | Source videos are third-party broadcasts; exact shared split and raw-video redistribution terms require clearance |
| Fine-Badminton temporal release | 31 professional singles matches, 2,104 rallies, 27,597 actions, 29 interval classes | 720p broadcast footage, resampled to 25 fps | Temporal onset/offset localization | Public Zenodo subset is ten matches; original copyright remains with content owners |
| BFMD | 19 full matches, 12 singles and 7 doubles; 1,054 singles rallies and 11,301 singles hits | Full BWF World Tour broadcasts; frame-level event annotations | Full-match segmentation, dense context, intent-like semantic fields | Source videos omitted; non-commercial academic use and non-redistribution restriction |
| VideoBadminton | 7,822 clips, 18 classes, 19 practice players, player and shuttle annotations | 1280×960, 60 fps, fixed camera | Controlled action-recognition baseline and frame-rate comparison | Practice data, controlled augmentation, and complete licensing details not fully stated |
| BadmintonDB | Nine matches between two players with rally, stroke, and outcome annotations | Video and access details limited in supplied abstract | Player-specific outcome and stroke baseline | Very small player population; not a complete four-component corpus |

The counts of ShuttleSet should not be merged indiscriminately. The release paper reports 44 matches and 27 players; the BST processing reports 40 cleaned matches and 33,429 strokes after exclusions; Wang’s ShuttleNet paper reports a separate 75-match, 31-player corpus with 43,191 strokes. These are materially different scopes.

The same caution applies to FineBadminton and Fine-Badminton. The former is a 2025 multi-level semantic dataset with 120 matches and 33,325 strokes; the latter is a 2026 temporal-localization benchmark with 31 matches, 29 categories, and 27,597 intervals. Their names are similar but their labels and temporal units are not interchangeable.

### Inclusion and exclusion criteria

For the shared four-component corpus, include:

- singles rallies with exactly one player on each side;
- the full rally from service contact to the shuttle becoming out of play;
- enough pre- and post-rally context to identify camera transitions;
- native frame rate, resolution, and source metadata;
- ordinary broadcast and practice footage, provided their source conditions are recorded.

Exclude from the primary rally set:

- doubles rallies;
- replay footage or duplicate angles unless explicitly marked as another view;
- advertisements, ceremonies, interviews, and non-play segments;
- unrelated matches visible in the background;
- clips where one player is absent for a source or editing reason;
- synthetic or controlled ball-feeding clips from the natural-play test set.

Do not delete difficult cases such as near-net overlap, blur, camera zoom, shadows, or shuttle loss. They should be retained and stratified. A separate “clean” subset can support debugging, but the main test set must represent deployment conditions.

### Camera and frame-rate metadata

Each video should record:

- native frame rate and any variable-frame-rate behavior;
- resolution and aspect ratio;
- camera position and angle when known;
- static, panning, zooming, or cut status;
- overhead, rear-court, side, or oblique viewpoint;
- court visibility and line quality;
- lighting, shadows, broadcast graphics, and spectators;
- whether the video is full-match, rally-clipped, or practice footage.

Frame annotations should be stored in seconds and native frame indices. If videos are resampled, retain the original timestamps and a deterministic conversion map. FineBadminton resamples broadcast material to 25 fps, while VideoBadminton records at 60 fps and Shishido and Nishijima convert their study videos to 30 fps. These differences make frame counts incomparable without time normalization.

### Split design

The primary split should be constructed at the match level before any temporal-window extraction:

- training matches;
- validation matches;
- test matches.

No rally, clip, frame window, or augmented copy from a match may cross splits. A stronger secondary protocol should also make players disjoint between training and test. A third protocol should hold out camera viewpoint, competition level, era, or source platform.

Report at least:

1. **Match-disjoint:** tests generalization to unseen matches but may contain known players.
2. **Player-disjoint:** tests unseen players and clothing or style changes.
3. **Cross-view or cross-source:** tests camera and collection shift.
4. **Rare-label stress test:** holds out or downweights rare and ambiguous categories according to a preregistered rule.

Existing datasets use materially different protocols. The Badminton Olympic dataset uses match- and player-disjoint splitting. FineBadminton semantic and BFMD releases provide rich data but do not, in the supplied evidence, establish one common match/player-disjoint split for all four tasks. ShuttleSet explicitly has no predefined train, validation, and test sets; some forecasting studies use the first 80% of each match’s rallies for training and the remainder for testing. Random 90%/10% splits, such as Yuan et al.’s outcome study, should not be treated as evidence of cross-match generalization.

### Annotation units and provenance

The annotation hierarchy should be:

1. match;
2. game or set;
3. rally;
4. stroke or hit event;
5. action interval;
6. player track frame;
7. tactical shot or rally unit;
8. next-action target.

Every annotation should record whether it was:

- manually created;
- generated by a detector or tracker;
- corrected by an expert;
- adjudicated;
- derived from other fields.

A model should never receive a derived label as if it were independent ground truth. For example, a hit frame generated from the same detector used as an input creates circular evaluation.

### Agreement and quality control

Tracking quality should be measured using box overlap, identity agreement, visible/occluded status agreement, court-coordinate error, and hit-actor agreement. A suitable subset should receive duplicate box and identity annotation.

Technical-action agreement should report Cohen’s kappa or a related categorical statistic, per-class agreement, temporal-boundary disagreement, and the adjudication rate. The Fine-Badminton temporal study reports more than 98% final inter-review agreement after senior review and professional-coach audits, but that is not a substitute for per-class agreement or tracking identity agreement.

Intent agreement requires a more demanding protocol because labels are subjective. Report the expert-agreement ceiling, confidence, uncertainty, and the proportion of samples for which experts abstain. Do not convert low agreement into artificial certainty by forcing an adjudicator to select one label without preserving the original disagreement.

### Licensing, privacy, and ethics

Public availability does not establish redistribution rights. BFMD provides annotations and helper scripts but omits source videos, which must be re-downloaded from BWF TV; it restricts use to non-commercial academic research and prohibits redistribution ([BFMD access terms](https://ning-d.github.io/BFMD-Dataset/)). The Fine-Badminton Zenodo release states that the original video copyright remains with the respective content owners and limits distribution to non-commercial academic research ([Fine-Badminton Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20292976)). Copyright Clearance Center guidance emphasizes that a dataset’s arrangement or compilation may be protected even when individual raw facts are not, and recommends checking terms and obtaining permission when unclear ([Copyright Clearance Center](https://www.copyright.com/blog/is-the-dataset-youre-using-protected-by-copyright-heres-how-to-find-out/)).

Before collection or redistribution, the project should document:

- the right to download, store, process, and publish derived annotations;
- whether source videos may be redistributed;
- whether screenshots, crops, pose data, or embeddings are considered derived material under the applicable terms;
- whether BWF, broadcaster, tournament, or platform conditions apply;
- whether institutional ethics or data-protection review is required;
- how identifiable faces, names, jersey numbers, and biometric-like representations are handled.

Anonymous `P_A` and `P_B` identities are sufficient for the core tasks. Named player identity should be optional and should not be introduced merely because it improves prediction. BFMD’s practice of anonymizing player identities as `[PLAYER]` is a useful privacy-preserving precedent.
